findings.title: Home/Study 'Review now' badge counts every never-studied card, contradicting the actual session and making 'All caught up' unreachable
findings.description: HomeView.dueCount and StudyHubView.dueCount (StudyHubView.swift:76) use LearningProgressStore.getDueCards, which returns every card whose masteryLevel == .new — i.e. the entire 15-card built-in deck plus every saved term that has never been introduced. The session started by 'Review now' (getCardsForReview) introduces at most dailyNewCardLimit (10/day) new cards and caps at 20 total. Scenario: a user with 100 saved words completes today's entire session; Home still shows 'Review now [~90]' and StudyHub shows 'Cards are waiting for you' with a huge badge. StudyHub's 'All caught up — great work' state cannot appear for weeks. The badge over-promises and never reconciles with what tapping it delivers.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the badge from the same logic as the session: due-with-history count + min(unseen count, remaining daily new-card budget), e.g. expose a `pendingReviewCount(from:)` on LearningProgressStore and use it in HomeView and StudyHubView.

findings.title: Dictation 'Slow' replay button plays at normal speed; the speakSlow API added in this same changeset has zero callers
findings.description: The tortoise-icon button labeled 'Slow' (accessibility 'Replay slowly') calls SpeechService.speakAuto(item.promptText) — byte-for-byte identical to the normal play button. A 中文-UI learner who can't catch an English word (or an English-UI learner parsing tones) taps 'Slow' and hears the exact same full-speed utterance; the control is a lie. The in-code comment claims 'SpeechService exposes a single rate', but this overhaul itself added SpeechService.speakSlow(_:languageCode:) (SpeechService.swift:27) which scales the persisted rate by 0.6 — and it has no callers anywhere (dead API).
findings.suggestedFix: Call the slow path with a content-matched voice: `SpeechService.speakSlow(item.promptText, languageCode: item.promptText.containsCJK ? "zh-CN" : "en-US")` (or add a speakAutoSlow helper). Delete the stale comment.

findings.title: Reader classifies any text containing a single CJK character as Chinese material, breaking English texts with incidental Chinese
findings.description: ReaderText.isChineseContent = content.containsCJK. A 中文-UI learner pastes an English article that mentions one Chinese name (e.g. '…in Beijing (北京)…'): the whole session renders through RubyTextView's Chinese pipeline instead of English word chips (ReaderSessionView.swift:195), vocabulary coverage is computed against the chineseSide of saved terms (ReaderVocabularyCoverage, line 138) so it reads ~0% known, and the library card shows wordCount as '2 characters' (only CJK ideographs counted) for an 800-word English article. Per-paragraph translation direction also flips to Chinese→English for English paragraphs.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a proportion threshold instead of presence: treat content as Chinese only when CJK ideographs are, say, >15–30% of letter-bearing characters (or majority-script detection via NLLanguageRecognizer). Apply the same rule in ReaderVocabularyCoverage.

findings.title: 'Practice this word' under Word of the Day starts a generic due-review session that usually does not contain the shown word
findings.description: The button triggers AppRouteStore.triggerReview(mode: "due", source: "home") — a generic session of due cards plus today's new-card budget (max 20). The daily word is a deterministic pick over the user's whole vocabulary (or the builtin deck), so it is typically NOT in that session: e.g. the word's next review is scheduled next week, or it is unseen but beyond the 10/day new-card budget. Both audiences tap a button promising to practice the displayed word and land in a flashcard session where it never appears.
findings.suggestedFix: Either route a targeted single-card session (extend startReview with a cardId that LearnView front-loads), or relabel honestly ('Start review' / 'Review due cards').

findings.title: iOS Home 'Stats' quick action and Recent Saves 'See All' dump the user on the Study hub root instead of the promised screen
findings.description: On iOS, the quick action labeled 'Stats' (line 366) and the Recent Saves header action 'See All' (line 454, which promises the vocabulary list) both just set selectedTab = .study, landing on StudyHubView's root. The user must then find Library → Stats / Library → Vocabulary themselves — two more taps with no signal about where the promised content lives. On macOS the same buttons route correctly (.stats / .vocabulary sidebar items), so this is an iOS-only broken promise. StudyHubView only auto-pushes a route for startReview pending actions, nothing else.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a pending StudyRoute to AppRouteStore (like startReview) and have StudyHubView push .stats / .vocabulary when it arrives, so these buttons deep-link on iOS as they do on macOS.

findings.title: Flashcard back shows Chinese-only example sentences to 中文-UI (English-learning) users — perspective-B gets no learning value from examples
findings.description: FlashcardView's back renders card.exampleSentence for both directions, but every built-in deck example is a Chinese sentence (LearningCard.swift:301-315). For an English-UI learner the example demonstrates the learning language (with pinyin — correct). For a 中文-UI learner the front is the English word being learned, and the back shows the Chinese meaning plus a Chinese example sentence: pure native-language furniture with zero English usage demonstrated. The one place perspective B would see the target word in context shows it only in their own language, making the deck's example feature an English-UI-only benefit.
findings.suggestedFix: Add English example sentences to the built-in deck (parallel field or bilingual pair) and show the learning-language example: Chinese+pinyin for learningChinese, English for 中文-UI users; hide the example when no learning-language version exists.

findings.title: High-priority DragGesture on Word Details ScrollView blocks vertical scrolling on iOS 17
findings.description: TermDetailSheet attaches .highPriorityGesture(DragGesture(minimumDistance: 40)) directly to the ScrollView. highPriorityGesture takes precedence over the view's own gestures — including the scroll pan — so on iOS 17 (the deployment floor) any drag over 40pt, vertical included, is claimed by the swipe-navigation gesture and the sheet stops scrolling. The horizontal-only guard (abs(dx) > 2*abs(dy)) runs in onEnded, i.e. after the touch is already claimed, so it cannot give the drag back to the ScrollView. The Word Details sheet regularly overflows one screen (headword + definition + AI Word Analysis), leaving iOS 17 users unable to reach content below the fold.
findings.suggestedFix: Use .simultaneousGesture instead of .highPriorityGesture (navigation still fires on clearly horizontal swipes and never steals vertical pans), or attach the gesture only to a non-scrolling header region. Verify on an iOS 17 simulator.

findings.title: SpeechService activates a ducking audio session it never deactivates, and category flip kills in-flight dictation
findings.description: configureAudioSessionForPlayback() runs before every utterance: setCategory(.playback, options: [.duckOthers]) + setActive(true), but nothing ever calls setActive(false). Ducking lasts as long as the session is active, so after a single 'Speak' tap the user's background music stays permanently quiet until the app is backgrounded or dictation deactivates the session. Worse, SpeechRecognitionService records with .playAndRecord and an active AVAudioEngine tap; in ConversationView the partner-bubble speaker button and DictationView's replay buttons are tappable while the mic is live — speaking then flips the category to .playback (no input), which breaks the running recognition tap and silently kills dictation.
findings.suggestedFix: Deactivate the session (setActive(false, options: .notifyOthersOnDeactivation)) when speech finishes via AVSpeechSynthesizerDelegate, and skip the category change (or stop recording first) when SpeechRecognitionService.isRecording.

findings.title: Dictation 'Slow' replay button plays at normal speed while speakSlow sits unused
findings.description: The tortoise button captioned 'Slow' with accessibility label 'Replay slowly' calls SpeechService.speakAuto(item.promptText) — identical to the adjacent normal play button. Its comment claims 'SpeechService exposes a single rate', but this same changeset added SpeechService.speakSlow(_:), which is now dead code (zero call sites repo-wide). A learner taps Slow to pick apart syllables/tones and hears the exact same utterance at the same rate — the feature's promise is not delivered on either platform, and VoiceOver users are explicitly told it replays slowly.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a speakAutoSlow (CJK-aware) variant or route the button through SpeechService.speakSlow with the detected language code; delete the stale comment.

findings.title: Menu-bar 'Open SwiftMandarin' cannot reopen a closed main window on macOS
findings.description: The footer button only calls NSApp.activate(). MenuBarExtra keeps the app alive after the user closes the main window (a normal menu-bar workflow), but activate() does not send a reopen event and SwiftUI does not recreate the WindowGroup window. Scenario: user closes the main window, uses the menu-bar quick translate, clicks 'Open SwiftMandarin' — the panel closes, the app becomes frontmost, and no window appears. The button is the panel's advertised path back into the full app and it dead-ends exactly when it is most needed.
findings.suggestedFix: Inject @Environment(\.openWindow), give the main WindowGroup an id, and call openWindow(id:) before NSApp.activate() so the main window is created if missing.

findings.title: New Practice haptics ignore the user's 'Haptic Feedback' setting
findings.description: PracticeHaptics.success()/error() fire UINotificationFeedbackGenerator unconditionally, while the established call sites in this same branch (TranslateView.triggerHaptic, VocabularyView.triggerHaptic) explicitly gate on the 'hapticFeedback' UserDefaults key (default true, with careful unset-key handling). A user who turns off Settings → Haptic Feedback still gets success/error buzzes on every answer in QuizView, DictationView, and TonePairDrillView — six call sites in the new Practice features bypass the documented preference the rest of the app honors.
findings.suggestedFix: Inside PracticeHaptics, read (UserDefaults.standard.object(forKey: "hapticFeedback") as? Bool) ?? true and return early when false, matching TranslateView.triggerHaptic.

findings.title: Repeat-forever pulse/typing animations ignore Reduce Motion (and CelebrationBurst still translates)
findings.description: ConversationChatView starts a .repeatForever scale pulse on the mic button (line 249, scaleEffect 1.15 at line 382) and TypingIndicatorBubble runs staggered .repeatForever blinking (line 611) with no accessibilityReduceMotion check, so users who enabled Reduce Motion get indefinite pulsing motion during every recording and every AI reply. CelebrationBurst (DesignSystem.swift:330) claims to honor Reduce Motion but only swaps spring for easeOut — the sparkles still translate outward 6→56pt, which is motion, not a fade. The lens' reference implementation is therefore also only partially compliant.
findings.suggestedFix: Read @Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion); skip the mic scale pulse (keep the red tint), keep the typing dots' opacity-only blink or make it static, and in CelebrationBurst keep radius fixed and animate opacity only when reduceMotion is true.

findings.title: TTS activates .duckOthers audio session and never deactivates it — background music stays ducked forever; category swap can kill an active dictation
findings.description: configureAudioSessionForPlayback() runs before EVERY utterance: setCategory(.playback, options: [.duckOthers]) + setActive(true), but nothing ever deactivates the session when speech finishes (no synthesizer delegate, no setActive(false)). Ducking lasts while the session is active, so on iOS: user listens to Music, taps any speaker button once → Music volume drops and STAYS reduced indefinitely (until they happen to use mic dictation, whose stopRecording at SpeechRecognitionService.swift:316 is the only deactivation path). Secondary hit: while dictating in ConversationView, tapping a partner bubble's speaker re-categorizes the session from .playAndRecord to .playback under the running AVAudioEngine input tap, which stops/breaks the in-flight recording.
findings.suggestedFix: Adopt AVSpeechSynthesizerDelegate (didFinish/didCancel) and call session.setActive(false, options: .notifyOthersOnDeactivation) when speech ends; skip re-categorizing when SpeechRecognitionService.isRecording (or use .playAndRecord-compatible playback while recording).

findings.title: Dictation 'Slow' replay button plays at normal speed; new speakSlow API is dead code
findings.description: The tortoise button (label "Slow", accessibility label "Replay slowly") calls SpeechService.speakAuto(item.promptText) — identical to the normal play button. The excusing comment ("SpeechService exposes a single rate") is stale: this same overhaul added SpeechService.speakSlow (rate × 0.6) at SpeechService.swift:27, which no caller uses (grep confirms zero call sites). A learner who taps 'Replay slowly' to pick apart tones hears the exact same utterance at the same speed — the feature the button promises does not exist, on every dictation round.
findings.suggestedFix: Route the tortoise button through the slow rate, direction-aware: item.promptText.containsCJK ? SpeechService.speakSlow(text, languageCode: "zh-CN") : SpeechService.speakSlow(text, languageCode: "en-US") (or add a speakSlowAuto). Delete the stale comment.

findings.title: Study hub Review badge shows uncapped backlog while Home and the actual session cap new cards — three contradictory due counts
findings.description: StudyHubView.dueCount uses progressStore.getDueCards(from:).count, which counts EVERY never-reviewed card (fresh CardProgress has nextReviewDate = now, and masteryLevel == .new also matches). HomeView.dueCount (HomeView.swift:96-110) deliberately caps new cards at the remaining dailyNewCardLimit budget (comment: counting the whole backlog "would be demoralizing"). User with 300 saved terms, none reviewed: Home says "~10 to review", the Study tab badge says "315", and tapping it opens a LearnView session of 20. The Study badge contradicts both the Home number and what the session actually contains, undermining the 'honest queue' the overhaul aims for.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute StudyHubView.dueCount the same way HomeView does: true due (reviewCount > 0 && nextReviewDate <= now) plus min(new backlog, remaining daily new-card budget). Consider extracting one shared helper on LearningProgressStore so the numbers can't diverge again.

findings.title: File-backed Reader/Conversation stores have no last-known-good backup: a top-level decode failure silently empties them and the next mutation overwrites the file
findings.description: PersistentCodableStore's UserDefaults path keeps a "<key>.backup" snapshot and restores from it on decode failure, but loadArrayFromFile (PersistentCodableStore.swift:120-132) has no equivalent: if reader-texts.json exists but its top-level JSON fails to parse (disk/iCloud-restore corruption, or a future build changing the top-level shape then downgrading), load() returns nil, texts starts empty, and the user's first add()/markOpened() atomically overwrites the file — permanently destroying every text they wrote and all chat history. Per-row tolerance (FailableDecodable + tolerant init(from:)) covers corrupt rows, but not this whole-file case. Acceptable for the regenerable word-explanation cache the pattern was copied from; ReaderStore/ConversationStore hold irreplaceable user content.
findings.suggestedFix: In loadArrayFromFile (or the two stores' load()), on a decode failure rename the corrupt file to "<name>.corrupt-<timestamp>" instead of leaving it to be overwritten, and/or write a "<name>.backup" copy after each successful load, mirroring the UserDefaults pipeline.
